For investors and founders, such acquisitions can represent major financial milestones. For employees holding equity compensation, a transaction can also change personal financial plans they had expected to follow for years. She compared the confusion to the atmosphere surrounding a major reorganization or a round of layoffs. The transaction offered the prospect of substantial financial gains. Yet employees were struggling to establish what those gains would mean for them individually. One acquisition, different outcomes Ron Honig, co-CEO of From-Honig Family Office. top_stories.title: ‘Weird And Maybe Uninvestable’: How Reach Capital Spots Its Venture Winners
top_stories.content: Before James Kim evaluated education startups, he used their products in his classroom. The Reach Capital partner began his career as a high school math teacher with Teach For America after studying astrophysics at Yale. He later worked in college access and Yale admissions, and earned graduate degrees in business and education from Stanford before joining Reach. As a teacher, he was an early user of ClassDojo, an experience he describes as “game-changing.” James Kim, partner at Reach Capital. (Courtesy photo) His investment firm, Reach Capital, has also evolved. Founded in 2015 after spinning out of NewSchools Venture Fund, the San Francisco-based firm initially focused on technology for K-12 schools and districts. Its mandate has since expanded to learning, health and work, with investments in companies including ClassDojo, Cartwheel, Stepful and Replit. In August, Reach announced its fifth fund, a $265 million vehicle that brought its assets under management to nearly $1 billion. The firm, which has backed more than 180 companies, plans to invest in approximately 50 additional teams through the new fund, targeting pre-seed, seed and Series A rounds. Crunchbase News spoke with Kim about how Reach’s education roots inform its broader strategy, what it saw in AI detection company GPTZero, and why some of its best investments initially divided its own team. We also discussed how ownership stakes and secondary transactions have shaped the firm’s approach to returning capital. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. items.title: AI for the Fortune 2000: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native SDLC — Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess
items.content: Last year, Alex Lieberman and his cofounder joined us to explain Tenex’s unusual bet: pay AI engineers for the work they deliver, rather than the hours they spend at a keyboard. If AI makes an engineer faster, an hourly rate can make the engineer less money for the same job. Tenex wanted the incentives to run the other way.At AIE New York, Alex came back with CJ Hess to talk about what happens when you scale that idea into an engineering organization. We also put one of our own experiments on the table: Kill My SaaS, where we asked builders to replace a conference speaker-management tool we were quoted $43,000 a year to use.Both stories raise the same question: when building gets cheaper, how do you decide what good work is worth?Paying for output when the job keeps changingTenex still uses story points as an important part of engineering compensation. Alex says the feared failure modes—people inflating estimates or shipping bad code to rack up points—haven’t been the biggest problem. Tenex’s AI strategists are responsible for customer retention and growth, giving them an incentive to push back on work that doesn’t serve the client.The harder question is how to reward work that doesn’t fit neatly into a ticket: understanding a customer’s problem, designing an architecture, or deciding what should be built in the first place. CJ describes spending less time directly coding as models get better, and more time getting the customer’s context into a form the model can use. A compensation system designed around shipped tasks has to make room for that work too.Alex says Tenex has grown to 75 people, with customers split between Fortune 2000 companies and mid-market businesses. The firm started as an AI-powered development shop; increasingly, customers are asking for help with AI transformation across the company. items.title: Enterprises keep buying software upgrades that IT thinks will make things worse
items.content: Enterprise-sized businesses spend, on average, 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes. Often, those firms' IT heads think those changes are detrimental. Those results are according to a survey of 2,018 chief information officers and senior IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees that Origina commissioned for its report, “The Software Tax.” About half of the respondents (1,011) are from the US, and the rest are from the United Kingdom. All respondents worked at companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue. Keep in mind that Origina provides maintenance for various enterprise software. Its report points to independent software maintenance as a way for IT leaders to regain control over software budgets, illustrating its potential bias. A third-party research consultancy, Censuswide, conducted the survey.Read full article Comments

items.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
items.content: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure: August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal. August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress. August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team. September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix. October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available. October 21

all_items.title: When A Startup Sells, Its Employees’ Equity Plans Can Change Overnight
all_items.content: By Ron Honig Acquisitions are reshaping the technology industry. Venture-backed AI companies acquired 195 AI startups this year through late September, already exceeding the total for all of 2025, Crunchbase data shows. For investors and founders, such acquisitions can represent major financial milestones. For employees holding equity compensation, a transaction can also change personal financial plans they had expected to follow for years. A client whose employer was acquired in an all-cash transaction described to me the atmosphere inside the company during the weeks that followed: Employees repeatedly discussed the deal in office corridors, trying to understand what it meant for their equity awards, their jobs and their future. She compared the confusion to the atmosphere surrounding a major reorganization or a round of layoffs. The transaction offered the prospect of substantial financial gains. Yet employees were struggling to establish what those gains would mean for them individually. One acquisition, different outcomes Ron Honig, co-CEO of From-Honig Family Office. Employees at the same company can emerge from an acquisition with remarkably different financial outcomes. Some own vested shares. Others hold restricted stock units, stock options or performance-based awards. Their rights depend on grant agreements, vesting conditions and transaction terms. Even two employees holding RSUs may face different payment schedules or employment requirements. Depending on the agreements, outstanding awards may be settled in cash, accelerated, converted into replacement awards, or remain subject to future conditions. One employee might receive a substantial payment when the transaction closes. Another may have much of the expected value tied to continued employment. The announced acquisition price provides a reference point. It rarely tells an individual employee everything they need to know about the money they will receive. all_items.title: ‘Weird And Maybe Uninvestable’: How Reach Capital Spots Its Venture Winners
all_items.content: Before James Kim evaluated education startups, he used their products in his classroom. The Reach Capital partner began his career as a high school math teacher with Teach For America after studying astrophysics at Yale. He later worked in college access and Yale admissions, and earned graduate degrees in business and education from Stanford before joining Reach. As a teacher, he was an early user of ClassDojo, an experience he describes as “game-changing.” James Kim, partner at Reach Capital. (Courtesy photo) His investment firm, Reach Capital, has also evolved. Founded in 2015 after spinning out of NewSchools Venture Fund, the San Francisco-based firm initially focused on technology for K-12 schools and districts. Its mandate has since expanded to learning, health and work, with investments in companies including ClassDojo, Cartwheel, Stepful and Replit. In August, Reach announced its fifth fund, a $265 million vehicle that brought its assets under management to nearly $1 billion. The firm, which has backed more than 180 companies, plans to invest in approximately 50 additional teams through the new fund, targeting pre-seed, seed and Series A rounds. Crunchbase News spoke with Kim about how Reach’s education roots inform its broader strategy, what it saw in AI detection company GPTZero, and why some of its best investments initially divided its own team. We also discussed how ownership stakes and secondary transactions have shaped the firm’s approach to returning capital. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. all_items.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
all_items.content: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. all_items.title: AI for the Fortune 2000: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native SDLC — Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess
all_items.content: Last year, Alex Lieberman and his cofounder joined us to explain Tenex’s unusual bet: pay AI engineers for the work they deliver, rather than the hours they spend at a keyboard. If AI makes an engineer faster, an hourly rate can make the engineer less money for the same job. Tenex wanted the incentives to run the other way.At AIE New York, Alex came back with CJ Hess to talk about what happens when you scale that idea into an engineering organization. We also put one of our own experiments on the table: Kill My SaaS, where we asked builders to replace a conference speaker-management tool we were quoted $43,000 a year to use.Both stories raise the same question: when building gets cheaper, how do you decide what good work is worth?Paying for output when the job keeps changingTenex still uses story points as an important part of engineering compensation. Alex says the feared failure modes—people inflating estimates or shipping bad code to rack up points—haven’t been the biggest problem. Tenex’s AI strategists are responsible for customer retention and growth, giving them an incentive to push back on work that doesn’t serve the client.The harder question is how to reward work that doesn’t fit neatly into a ticket: understanding a customer’s problem, designing an architecture, or deciding what should be built in the first place. CJ describes spending less time directly coding as models get better, and more time getting the customer’s context into a form the model can use. A compensation system designed around shipped tasks has to make room for that work too.Alex says Tenex has grown to 75 people, with customers split between Fortune 2000 companies and mid-market businesses. The firm started as an AI-powered development shop; increasingly, customers are asking for help with AI transformation across the company. all_items.title: Enterprises keep buying software upgrades that IT thinks will make things worse
all_items.content: Enterprise-sized businesses spend, on average, 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes. Often, those firms' IT heads think those changes are detrimental. Those results are according to a survey of 2,018 chief information officers and senior IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees that Origina commissioned for its report, “The Software Tax.” About half of the respondents (1,011) are from the US, and the rest are from the United Kingdom. All respondents worked at companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue. Keep in mind that Origina provides maintenance for various enterprise software. Its report points to independent software maintenance as a way for IT leaders to regain control over software budgets, illustrating its potential bias. A third-party research consultancy, Censuswide, conducted the survey.Read full article Comments
